chunks: "The rule for a motor is that current is highest when the back-EMF is lowest relative to the applied voltage, because the current is V minus K e omega over R.
So the biggest currents come from a few situations. First, startup and stall: speed zero, so about V over R, 12 amps for 12 volts and 1 ohm.
Second, any heavy load or jam that holds the speed down.
Third, and bigger than people expect, direction reversal, or plugging: if you flip the supply polarity while it's spinning at full speed, the back-EMF now adds to the supply instead of opposing it.
At 575 rad/s that's 12 plus 11. 5 volts across 1 ohm, so 23. 5 amps, almost twice the stall current. Also braking by shorting the winding gives K e omega over R, around 11.
5 amps at full speed, and in a bridge, shoot-through can be hundreds of amps for microseconds.
For solenoids, the max is the steady state V over R once the coil's current has settled; some drivers deliberately overdrive during pull-in with a higher voltage for a stronger, faster pull.
AC solenoids draw several times their holding current when the plunger is open.
And there are modifiers: a cold coil has lower resistance so more current, low supply or high source resistance lowers it but makes the rail sag, and PWM ripple adds a peak above the average.
So I size the driver and supply for the worst case, plugging or shoot-through, and I use current limits, soft start and dead-time to keep it under control."
